title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you persuaded someone without authority"?
description: How to answer persuasion and influence questions in consulting interviews, with weak and strong examples and what interviewers look for.
hook: You answer "Tell me about a time you persuaded someone without authority" with a story that shows you understood why the other person resisted, then lowered the risk for them, often with a small test, and let evidence change their mind. Consultants spend their days persuading people they do not manage, including senior clients. This question tests whether you can do that with care rather than pressure.
body:
What the interviewer is testing

A client manager does not have to do what a junior consultant suggests. The interviewer wants to see that you can bring people round anyway. At McKinsey this sits close to what the firm calls personal impact, and its interviewing page frames one prompt around a disagreement with someone who held an opposing view. The details they listen for:

  • Did you find out why the other person disagreed?
  • Did you adapt your approach to their concern, rather than repeating your argument louder?
  • Did they end up owning the decision?

A weak answer

I had to convince my manager to use my idea. I explained it really clearly and showed him it was better, and eventually he agreed.

Why it falls short: the other person's view is missing, the method is just "explaining clearly", there is no result, and the person persuaded was the speaker's manager, which is not really "without authority" in the sense the question means.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use your own.

Our operations lead didn't want to change the delivery schedule I was proposing, even though my analysis showed it would save money. Instead of pushing, I asked what worried him. It turned out late deliveries had hurt his team's performance reviews before, and he saw my plan as a risk to him, not a saving. So I proposed a two-week trial on one route, with him choosing the route and deciding what counted as success. Deliveries stayed on time and costs on that route fell 8%. He presented the results to his director himself, and the schedule went to every route the next month.

Why it works: it shows listening, understanding the other side's real concern, reducing their risk and giving them ownership, with a clear outcome. If you can, put the result in money too. If delivery costs across all routes were $500k a year, an 8% saving would be 0.08 × $500k = $40k a year.

The four-step sequence

Almost every good persuasion story follows the same order:

  1. Listen to the objection. Find out what the person is worried about, which is often not what they first say.
  2. Find a shared measure. Agree what success looks like in terms they care about.
  3. Lower the risk of trying. A pilot, a trial on one team, a clear way to stop.
  4. Let evidence decide. Share the results, ideally with them first, so the decision is theirs.

Here is a second illustrative story that follows it. A candidate on an operations project proposed an extra parcel scan at a warehouse handoff. The shift manager objected because his team was already under pressure to hit throughput targets. Rather than repeating that the scan would improve data, the candidate watched the handoff and found that searching for lost parcels was eating time later in the shift. They proposed a two-day test on one shift, agreed to stop if throughput fell, and tracked both parcels per hour and missing-parcel incidents. The error rate fell from 3.0% to 1.2% with no real change in throughput, and the manager backed a wider rollout.

The candidate did not win the argument. They changed the question from "your data or my targets" to "can we have both?", and tested it.

Prepare for the follow-ups

  • "What would you have done if the pilot had failed?"
  • "Did the manager have a legitimate concern?"
  • "How did you make sure they didn't feel overruled?"

Good answers show conviction balanced with a willingness to change your plan. Admitting that the other person had a fair point, and that your proposal improved because of it, makes the story stronger.

Common mistakes

  • The instant convert. If the person agreed after your first slide, there was no persuasion. Choose a story with real resistance.
  • Persuading by pressure. Going over someone's head or wearing them down is not what the interviewer wants to hear.
  • Ignoring their side. If you cannot explain why they disagreed, you have not finished preparing the story.
  • No outcome. If there is no number, describe what visibly changed: a decision made, a process adopted.

Try it now

1. A finance director refuses to fund your team's new tool. What is your first move?

Show the answer

Ask what worries her: cost, risk, timing, or a past project that failed. Then shape the proposal around that concern, for example a three-month trial with a fixed budget and agreed success measures she sets.

2. Your story ends: "Eventually they saw I was right." How would you improve it?

Show the answer

Show what changed their mind and give them credit: "After the two-week trial showed no drop in quality, she agreed to roll it out and presented it to her team herself." Persuasion stories land better when the other person ends up owning the decision.

3. Write your own story in four sentences, one for each step: the objection, the shared measure, the low-risk test, and the result.

Show the answer

Check the first sentence names the other person's real concern, not just that they disagreed. Check the third sentence makes it easy for them to say yes. If either is missing, the story will sound like you simply argued harder.

Where to practise next

Persuasion overlaps with leadership through difficulty and your biggest achievement, so make sure each story has a different focus. Map them all with the fit interview guide, and read the McKinsey interview process guide if you are applying there.
